Unravelling the energy performance gap: Understanding user-related factors affecting 
lighting energy consumption in office buildings 
 
Sascha Hammes 1, *, Johannes Weninger 2, Philipp Zech 3, Philipp Gschwandtner 3 
1 University of Innsbruck, Unit of Energy Efficient Building, Innsbruck, Austria 
2 Bartenbach, research & development, Wattens, Austria 
3 University of Innsbruck, Department of Computer Science, Innsbruck, Austria  
*Corresponding Author: sascha.hammes@uibk.ac.at  
 
 
Abstract 
The main cause of energy performance gaps is occupancy 
behaviour, which is difficult to predict. A breakdown of 
the defining characteristics, their weighting and range can 
help to counteract performance deficits. The effects of 
user-related influences on energy efficiency were 
analyzed 
using 
high-performance 
computing 
and 
probabilistic methods. This was based on high-resolution 
measurement data from an open-plan office, collected 
over the course of a year. The results show that both 
individual behaviour and the seating position have a 
significant influence on energy consumption. The 
findings help to improve simulations and plan more 
energy-efficient buildings. 
Key Innovations 
• Application of modern stochastic methods and high-
performance computing to analyse measurement data  
• Understanding the influence of occupancy behaviour 
and its determining characteristics  
• Basics for improving simulations and energy 
optimisation measures after commissioning 
Practical Implications 
Using probabilistic analyses, the fluctuations in lighting 
energy consumption could be traced back to user 
distributions. In addition to an understanding of formative 
factors, the results also illustrate methods for deriving 
optimised user distributions in the office space. 
Introduction 
Actual operation often has a higher energy demand than 
calculated during planning. This can usually be attributed 
to inefficient system operation. Despite the use of 
advanced modelling methods and energy-efficient 
technologies, buildings often fail to meet energy saving 
targets. As some studies report, buildings can even 
consume three times the energy demand calculated in the 
design phase (Liang et al., 2019; Zou and Alam, 2020). 
This becomes visible via the Energy Performance Gap 
(EPG), the difference between the actual energy 
consumption and the simulated forecasts (Liang et al., 
2019; Niu et al., 2015). Accurately planning building 
performance and achieving energy goals requires an 
understanding of and quantification of error causes. With 
the building sector using around a third of energy, 
efficient operation is becoming ever more important 
(UNEP, 2009). 
For these reasons, numerous research activities have 
already been carried out in the past to identify and 
eliminate the causes of the EPG (Liang et al., 2019; Niu 
et al., 2015; Zou et al., 2019; Zou and Alam, 2020). 
Deviations can arise during operation and in the planning 
process. Operation-related deviations include a lack of 
fine-tuning of control systems and suboptimal settings of 
technical systems (which occur when new technologies 
are first used (Zou et al., 2019)), inaccuracies in relevant 
measurement technology, deviations and errors in the 
execution work and inadequate use of equipment by the 
building users (Menezes et al., 2012). Van Dronkelaar et 
al. (2016) identifies specification uncertainties in building 
modelling as a major cause of planning errors. These 
include inaccuracies in the geometric representation as 
well 
as 
inaccurately 
stored 
material 
properties. 
Furthermore, in the context of the building design phase, 
unrealistic assumptions, and forecasting errors in the 
climate data (Erba et al., 2017). It has been shown that the 
uncertainty of the occupancy behaviour determines the 
failure or success of the statements made in the building 
design phase regarding the subsequent energy system 
performance (Niu et al., 2015). The cause of the EPG is 
often a combination of many of the aspects mentioned (de 
Wilde, 2014). 
The essential role of occupant behaviour on energy 
demand (Yoshino et al., 2017) is embodied in the fact that 
there is hardly any information on occupant behaviour 
during the building planning phase (Liang et al., 2019; 
Menezes et al., 2012). As a result, assumptions are made 
about occupancy behaviour. These are currently based on 
empirically proven and standardized models and are 
formulated as generally as possible to ensure a high 
degree of applicability, for example differentiation 
according to room type (sia, 2006). The dynamics of 
occupancy behaviour in the workplace are largely 
determined by the work activities and social conditions 
that define the organisation. As work processes and social 
conditions can vary greatly between organisations, the 
dynamics of occupancy can also vary greatly between 
organisations. In their study, Zhou et al. analyse temporal 
patterns in the artificial lighting energy demand of office 
buildings and find that energy consumption is highly 
stochastic (Zhou et al., 2015). This is not reflected in 
generalised occupancy models. Generally valid models 
seem to fail particularly when the social structure allows 
a lot of freedom, for example flexitime regulations and 
home office, see (Hammes et al., 2021a; Hammes et al.,

Uncertainties that must be closed to avoid inefficient 
building operation and secure energy goals. For this 
reason, some research efforts have already been carried 
out on this in the past. 
Related work 
To obtain a better picture of potential occupant behaviour 
as early as the planning phase, Niu et al. use an 
observation approach based on virtual reality (VR) 
technology in conjunction with digital building models 
and the Design with Intent (DwI) method. In iterative 
processes, building planners can use user-oriented VR 
experiments to analyse behavioural patterns, such as 
human-environment interaction, in the building model in 
advance and check whether these correspond to the 
specified design conditions and then adapt design 
strategies (Niu et al., 2015). The derivation of improved 
methods for modelling occupant behaviour and their 
implementation in simulation environments has also been 
the subject of past and current research activities within 
the International Energy Agency's Energy in Buildings 
and Communities Program (IEA EBC; see Yoshino et al. 
(2017)). However, there is still a lack of suitable 
quantification of the factors influencing user-related 
energy demand. 
Based on a survey of US facility managers, Liang et al. 
developed incentive schemes and energy performance 
contracts as well as methods to encourage more energy-
conscious behaviour change among occupants. This 
should encourage the closure of performance gaps after 
commissioning (Liang et al., 2019). In addition, Liang et 
al. identified and analysed organisational, behavioural, 
and technical factors influencing the EPG. Zou and Alam 
define a methodical collaboration framework where, 
using the example of an office building, the causes of EPG 
are identified, relevant responsibilities are involved (e.g. 
facility management, service companies, architecture) 
and dedicated investigations and measures are carried out. 
Post-occupancy evaluation (POE) not only provides a 
better understanding of EPGs and how to reduce them, but 
also feeds knowledge back into the planning process to 
reduce performance gaps in advance (Zou and Alam, 
2020). 
Objective of the study 
The literature states that the uncertainty of occupancy 
behaviour determines the failure or success of the 
statements made in the building planning phase regarding 
the subsequent energy performance of the system. 
Although previous studies have recognised the existence 
of this gap, the precise measurement of its extent remains 
a complex task due to various influencing factors. The 
aim of this study is therefore to comprehensively quantify 
the energy performance gap using lighting as an example 
by examining the effects of individual occupancy 
behavior at the workplace and the illuminance. The data 
is based on operational data from a real open-plan office, 
where high-resolution data was collected over a period of 
one year. 
Methodology 
Study object and data measurement 
The 160 m² open-plan office of the research and 
development (R&D) building of Bartenbach GmbH in 
Aldrans, Austria, is used as the study object (Figure 1, 
area marked in orange). The open-plan office can 
accommodate a maximum of 28 workstations. To ensure 
optimum operation and comfort, it is primarily operated 
for 18 people, who are distributed across nine workstation 
zones. Four zones for two people each are located on the 
north side along the skylight and five further workstation 
zones, each for two people as standard and a maximum of 
four people, along the south façade (see Figure 1). 
In the test object, the daylight and artificial lighting 
system is controlled separately for each workstation zone. 
In the context of energy-efficient lighting, there is 
presence control based on passive infrared sensors (PIR). 
The PIR sensor system is associated with switch-off times 
to reduce false off rates that impair comfort (Maniccia et 
al., 2001). Even though concepts have already been 
implemented in the study object to adapt these to 
occupancy behaviour for energy efficiency reasons 
(Hammes et al., 2021a), the present study works with an 
industry standard of 15 minutes (Garg and Bansal, 2000). 
In addition, the artificial light in the open-plan office is 
controlled via 
table-mounted 
illuminance 
sensors 
depending  on  the  availability  of  daylight.  There  is  an

option for manual control. Furthermore, to support the 
circadian rhythm, there is a colour-temperature control 
that is dynamically adapted to the time of day, from 
5000 K in the morning to 2200 K in the evening. The 
study building is characterized by a high level of daylight 
integration. On an annual average, horizontal illuminance 
levels of over 500 lx occur at workplaces between 09:00 
and 16:00. This means that the use of artificial light is 
primarily limited to the morning and evening hours, see 
(Hammes et al., 2021a; Hammes et al., 2022). To avoid 
glare and overheating, there are automatically controlled 
shading systems as well as external static daylight slats.  
Presence at each workstation and lighting levels per 
workstation zone are recorded by the building's control 
system. In addition, dimming levels and energy 
consumption are recorded to provide a complete picture 
of the lighting system's operation. Two women and 16 
men participated in the study. In order to avoid conflicts 
with data protection regulations, a voluntary declaration 
of consent was obtained from all users at whose 
workstations the occupancy profile was recorded and 
analysed. The measurement data and results are published 
in pseudonymised form. The core working hours during 
the study period were Monday to Thursday 9:00–12:00 
and 14:00–17:00 and Fridays from 9:00–12:00. 
Furthermore, as an organizational framework, there is the 
possibility of home office and a flexitime arrangement, 
which also contribute significantly to user dynamics. The 
measurement period per study day was set at 6:00–20:00. 
to accommodate flexitime work. The study was 
conducted outside the influence of COVID-19. The data 
was collected over a period of one year (February 2022 to 
January 2023) and compared with the simulated energy 
demand as part of the quantification of the EPG. 
A simulation is carried out to calculate reference results 
with which the different user distributions (based on 
measured values) are compared. For the simulation, the 
study object was modelled in a high level of detail using 
Rhinoceros 3D (version: Rhino 6). Honeybee[+], a 
Grasshopper plug-in in Rhinoceros, with RADIANCE as 
the daylight simulation engine was used as the simulation 
platform. Illuminance levels depending on the room 
position were generated in RADIANCE with EnergyPlus 
weather files. To use bidirectional scattering distribution 
functions (BSDF; generated for the study object via 
WINDOW7), an annual daylight simulation was carried 
out according to the three-phase method. Using the 
lighting simulation, a daylight autonomy (DA) of 81.56% 
was achieved in relation to the normative illuminance of 
500 lx and at a reference time of 8:00–18:00 (excluding 
summer time) - detailed results in (Hammes et al., 2021b). 
Shading was taken into account while maintaining the 
necessary glare protection. For the following comparative 
calculation, a reference time of 6:00–20:00 was used 
analogue to the sensor-based measurement series. Using 
an evaluation tool written in Python (version Python 3.10, 
pandas 2.0.0) and measured lighting performance 
profiles, the resulting energy consumption is determined 
and matched with the presence profiles for planning 
according to (sia, 2006). 
User distribution in the room 
The parameter relevant to the study is the artificial 
lighting energy demand of the individual workplace 
zones, as a product of the workplace-related presence 
information and the necessary artificial lighting 
supplementation to fulfil the normative minimum 
illuminance of 500 lx for office activities. Depending on 
the room position, the building geometry and orientation 
result in different levels of artificial lighting required in 
the individual workstation zones depending on the time. 
Furthermore, the artificial lighting requirement of an 
individual lighting zone results from the combined 
presence profile of two users, i.e. from the logical OR link 
matched with the position-dependent energy profile (see 
Figure 1 marked zone, users A and B). The greater the 
overlap time in energy-relevant times, the more 
efficiently the lighting zone is utilised. 
The derivation of an energy-optimised occupancy scheme 
for the described setting in the study object with 18 people 
results in a combinatorial assignment problem. There are 
153 possible user pairings that can be distributed 
differently to new zones without multiple utilisations of a 
user. This results in 12.5*1012 possible combinations. In 
order to investigate the effects of individual occupancy 
behavior and organizational structures at the workplace 
on the energy consumption of the open-plan office 
described and thus make a contribution to quantifying 
these influencing factors within the framework of the 
EPG, it is necessary to take sufficient account of the 
existing variety of combinations. Given the complexity, a 
representative sample (i.e. a specific distribution of user 
combinations and their positioning in the room) can only 
be calculated using high-performance computing. 
Data generation by high-performance computing 
The 
computational 
problem 
has 
no 
significant 
communication or synchronization required among 
individual samples, thereby posing a Monte-Carlo-type 
HPC class. For this reason, the sample generation and 
subsequent computation were parallelized using Python’s 
multiprocessing capabilities. The entire problem space 
was subdivided into batches to be executed in parallel on 
128 cores. Each batch ran for a wall time of approximately 
20 hours, and multiple batches were run on multiple 
compute nodes simultaneously. The total experiment time 
took approximately 60,000 core hours for generating and 
processing 10.24 million samples. There were no 
repetitions of samples.  
Despite being a compute-heavy problem (the maximum 
resident set size in RAM for each batch was below 20 MB 
per core), the computation generates a lot of data. Each 
batch originally produced approximately 80 GB of CSV 
output, which was reduced to 40 GB by changing to a 
Pickle-based format, Python’s idiomatic way of 
serializing data. Nevertheless, the total amount of output 
data still amounts to 440 GB.

The experiments were conducted on VSC-5 of the Vienna 
Scientific Cluster, the national supercomputing center of 
Austria. A tier-1 supercomputer, VSC-5 is equipped with 
770 nodes each consisting of two AMD EPYC 7713 
Milan Processors and a total of 128 cores along with 512 
GB of main memory.  
Evaluation methods 
The artificial light energy consumption of different 
occupancy schemes generated using HPC was compared 
with the energy consumption determined using simulation 
for different time of day and seasonal periods. The same 
was done regarding the room position. Stochastic 
methods were used to comprehensively quantify the 
associated effects on energy performance. The deviations 
between simulation and reality are analysed with regard 
to occupancy at the workplace and illuminance, as well as 
in combination. The influence on the energy demand 
corresponds to 100% for presence and 0% for absence. 
For illuminance (100% at 0 lx daylight, 0% at 500 lx). For 
the coupled influence, the deviation per zone is 
determined by subtracting the real value from the 
simulation value, whereby 0% stands for no energy 
demand and 100% for maximum energy demand. To 
identify outliers in the data and exclude them in detailed 
analyses, the 1.5 interquartile range (IQR) is used. 
Descriptive view of HPC-generated samples 
10.24 million samples were generated via HPC. Each 
sample contains a clear allocation of user combinations 
and workplaces, as well as the average energy 
consumption per hour and month associated with that 
combination, and the total energy consumption for the 
year. A frequency distribution of the cumulative artificial 
lighting energy demand of the individual samples over the 
academic year leads to a distribution that can be viewed 
as approximately normally distributed (Figure 2). The 
quantile-quantile diagram (Q-Q) is used to check for 
normal distribution (Figure 3), since other statistical tests, 
such as the Shapiro-Wilk test, are only designed for 
comparatively small sample sizes (Rahman and 
Govindarajulu, 1997). The excess kurtosis here is -0.192. 
The negative excess kurtosis indicates lighter tails and a 
flatter peak than in the normal distribution. The frequency 
distribution results in a mean value with a standard 
deviation of 238.64±12.31 kWh. For the 10.24 million 
samples, an occupancy scheme was identified with a 
minimum artificial lighting energy demand in the 
workplace zones of 182.81 kWh and, in the unfavourable 
case, with a maximum energy demand of 284.69 kWh. 
This results in a range of 101.88 kWh (maximum-
minimum). For the study setting, the expected artificial 
lighting energy demand based on real measured values 
and HPC-generated occupancy schemes is in the range of 
230.36 kWh (lower quantile, Figure 2) and 247.43 kWh 
(upper quantile). The measured values for the real 
situation in the study object led to an energy demand of 
237.32 kWh. Using the generally valid simulation 
assumptions for weather and occupancy (EnergyPlus 
weather file and (sia, 2006)), the artificial lighting energy 
demand for the workplaces is only 171.7 kWh for the 
year. Compared to the real measured energy demand, this 
corresponds to an absolute percentage deviation of 
38.22%, or 39.25%, from the median of the samples 
(239.1 kWh). The low artificial light energy consumption 
is due to the high daylight availability in the study 
property (DA=81.56%). A check for equal distribution of 
the 153 possible user pairings across the nine workstation 
zones shows that on average 66,928 user pairings were 
distributed per zone (minimum: 66,199; maximum: 
67,672; standard deviation: 252.32, cf. Figure 4). There is 
no limitation from the randomly generated samples.

Results 
The influencing factor occupancy 
A frequency distribution of the resulting hourly deviations 
is shown in Figure 5. This results in a clear peak in small 
deviations (around 175k comparison hours between 0 and 
+10%). 41.39% of all hourly deviations lie in the lower 
quantile (Q3, here -19.99%) and upper quantile (Q1, here 
20.0%). However, individual stronger swings in the 
positive and negative range can also be identified, up to 
+80% and -100%. To check their influence over time of 
day, the average of the hourly deviations of all 153 
possible user pairings, including the standard deviation, is 
plotted for the deviations in the quantile and for the 
deviations greater/less than 50% over the course of the 
day (Figure 6). The results show that the higher deviations 
(x>50% and x<-50%) are mainly in the periods from 
8:00–11:00 and between 13:00–17:00. These are the 
times in the study object when employees are mainly in 
meetings. Times when simulation and measurements 
show smaller deviations are, for example, at 12:00 and 
16:00. These times are representative of break times, 
which are also well represented by simulation models. 
The deviations considered within the quantile show peaks 
in the early morning (6:00–7:00) and late evening (18:00–
19:00), which can be explained by the fact that people use 
the flexitime regulation at these times (utilization rate per 
day and per person: 23.2% in the morning, 18.92% in the 
evening), which are not used in simulation models. 
 
Figure 5: Frequency distribution of deviations between 
the simulation assumptions and measured values

To analyse the temporal influences of the deviations in 
presence, the average of all deviations between simulation 
and real measured values is plotted depending on the time 
of day and the individual months (Figure 7). The standard 
deviation of the individual values is shown in colour. 
Over the year, the simulation overestimates attendance 
between 9:00–11:00 and between 13:00–16:00. The 
simulation underestimates attendance in the early 
morning hours and late evening hours. This makes it clear 
that simulation assumptions have difficulty absorbing 
work-specific occupancy dynamics such as meeting 
proportions and aspects such as flexitime regulations. 
Between the summer and winter months, there is a greater 
underestimation in the edge areas of the day, which can 
be attributed to the fact that the option to use flexitime is 
more widely perceived here.

The influencing factor illuminance 
The frequency distribution of all resulting hourly 
deviations in illuminance for all nine workplace zones 
(Figure 2) shows that the distribution is slightly shifted to 
the left (median: 0.0, lower quantile: 10.10, upper

the resulting hourly deviations that lie within the quantile

average illuminance levels greater than 500 lx occur in the 
daylight office. Deviations above this limit are irrelevant 
to artificial lighting energy consumption. Most critical 
deviations are identified in the edge areas of the day 
(orange characteristic curve, Figure 9). Split by time and 
month, the deviations between the illuminance values

Discussion 
The results of the artificial lighting energy demand for the 
individual user combinations, generated via HPC, show 
few to no outliers, which, in combination with the high 
number of samples, suggests that the distribution is well 
approximated and can be used as a starting point for this 
study. The influence of illuminance in the flexitimes is 
shown in the results. This can be explained by the fact that 
weather data for the simulation is usually only available 
in hourly resolution, which is less tragic for thermal 
simulation evaluation (as a trade with planning usually 
over several time steps) than for the lighting trade, where 
operations require a high temporal resolution, as the 
subsequent application must also be real-time capable. 
The hourly resolution of weather data increases the risk of 
incorrect assumptions being made at off-peak times. This 
is where the greatest deviations can be identified in the 
results. Higher-resolution data is therefore required for 
lighting simulations to consider dynamic changes in 
daylight-based illuminance. 
In addition to the illuminance, a defining factor identified 
is a high occupancy time in the work zone in the morning 
and evening hours, resulting either from a single person 
with high attendance or from the resulting profile of two 
users with little overlap time (logical OR link), is 
identified as a formative factor. Gaps in terms of 
attendance can also be defined on mostly hourly 
resolutions of occupancy models for the simulation. 
Dynamic processes are difficult to map here. In this study, 
a switch-off time of 15 min (orientated to the industry 
standard, cf. (Garg and Bansal, 2000) was used for the 
artificial light in the event of absence detection via the PIR 
sensor system, which corresponds to the industry 
standard. A stronger adaptation of the run-on time to real 
presence patterns (e.g., implemented in (Hammes et al., 
2021a) would lead to higher presence gaps. 
The work presented represents a POE and emphasises its 
suitability for drawing conclusions after commissioning 
to improve planning and simulation and thus reduce EPGs 
and, furthermore, to derive measures to improve energy 
consumption after commissioning. The classification 
methodology described above could be populated via 
POE studies to provide a better basis for planning. 
Limitations 
This study focuses exclusively on artificial lighting. 
However, the influence of heating, ventilation, and air 
conditioning (HVAC) systems on energy consumption of 
buildings is also high and strongly affected by occupancy 
dynamics. While the applied methodology of HPC can, in 
principle, be transferred to HVAC systems, it requires 
additional sensor and actuator data, which were not 
collected in the field study. The results could be applied 
in the HVAC sector to adapt ventilation and heating 
schedules to actual occupancy patterns, thus avoiding 
energy losses during periods of low use. Future work 
should investigate how similar deviations manifest in 
HVAC systems to better integrate occupancy behavior in 
energy efficiency simulations across domains.

Conclusion 
In synopsis, the generated dataset of 10.24 million HPC 
samples revealed a nearly normal distribution of artificial 
lighting energy demand, with an expected range of 
230.36–247.43 kWh, closely matching the real measured 
value of 237.32 kWh. However, standard simulation 
assumptions underestimated energy demand by up to 
39.25%, emphasizing the critical influence of real-world 
occupancy patterns and daylight availability. 
The study further investigates the factors that affect 
energy performance gaps, in particular weather data, 
attendance and lighting intensity. The temporal influences 
of the predictor deviations in lighting intensity and 
attendance on the EPG were identified using statistical 
analyses. Lighting intensity in particular has a strong 
influence on the extent of the EPG during the 
organisationally permissible flexitime. The results help to 
better understand the EPG in the lighting context and to 
quantify its influencing variables. 
Outlook 
Technologies such as HPC have made it possible to 
decipher the causes of the EPG. It was also possible to 
identify distributions that lead to the lowest possible 
energy demand (182.81 kWh). Approximation methods 
for determining energetically optimized occupancy 
schemes, based on graph theory methods, are presented in 
(Hammes et al., 2022). The algorithm identified a user 
distribution requiring only 178.32 kWh (2.46% deviation 
from the sample minimum) , highlighting its potential for 
optimizing space use and enabling further system 
improvements. HPC is another method. A method 
comparison is needed to assess practical suitability.

Abstract: The main cause of energy performance gaps is occupancy behaviour, which is difficult to predict. A breakdown of the defining characteristics, their weighting and range can help to counteract performance deficits. The effects of user-related influences on energy efficiency were analyzed using high-performance computing and probabilistic methods. This was based on high-resolution measurement data from an open-plan office, collected over the course of a year. The results show that both individual behaviour and the seating position have a significant influence on energy consumption. The findings help to improve simulations and plan more energy-efficient buildings. Key Innovations • Application of modern stochastic methods and high- performance computing to analyse measurement data • Understanding the influence of occupancy behaviour and its determining characteristics • Basics for improving simulations and energy optimisation measures after commissioning Practical Implications Using probabilistic analyses, the fluctuations in lighting energy consumption could be traced back to user distributions. In addition to an understanding of formative factors, the results also illustrate methods for deriving optimised user distributions in the office space.
